body:
[V6.5 General Multi-factor authentication requirements (as of time of this issue)](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x15-V6-Authentication.md#v65-general-multi-factor-authentication-requirements):

This may seem pedantic, but what are the storage requirements for email OTP? Given the word "password" is in the name, I'd assume it's subject to the same requirements as a password. However, the code is short-lived and this may not be a requirement. Hashing it forces a couple of behaviours that I think are good. For example, you wouldn't be able to resend the code, you'd have to issue a new if the user can receive the first.

I'd love to get guidance from OWASP on this one. Thanks!

comments.body:
An email OTP is definitely an authentication secret, so I’d treat it with “password-like” care: short TTL, single use, no logging, and no long-term plaintext storage.

Hashing OTPs is still useful, but not for the same reason as passwords. The number of possible codes is often tiny (like 1M for a 6-digit code, 100M for a 8-digit code), so a DB attacker can brute-force any hash instantly.

In practice, I’d:

* Generate a random OTP with sufficient entropy behind the scenes.
* Consider 8 digit codes or more.
* Store only a Argon2id or HMAC hash plus expiration date and attempt counter.
* Invalidate on success or too many tries.
* On “resend,” generate a new one and overwrite the old record.

That gives you good hygiene without pretending that OTP hashes give you the same kind of offline protection as real password hashes.

I think the fact that it is timelimited and has a relatively small number of options is why we don't mention specific security requirements.

> For example, you wouldn't be able to resend the code, you'd have to issue a new if the user can receive the first.

This is indeed a cool side effect although if I was building this I would probably want to think a bit about the potential threat scenarios before implementation.

That all makes sense to me and thanks for the response! This is really helpful. 

If you don't mind clarifying a couple of points for me:

> Hashing OTPs is still useful, but not for the same reason as passwords.

What are the reasons it's still useful? Just want to make sure I'm not misinterpreting. I assume it's still useful because storing any kind of password in plain-text isn't advisable. Are there other reasons?

> Store only a Argon2id or HMAC hash plus expiration date and attempt counter

Do you recommend Argon2id or HMAC hash for any particular reason? Is bcrypt valid?

> I think the fact that it is timelimited and has a relatively small number of options is why we don't mention specific security requirements.

That makes sense to me. I got into a lengthy debate about hashing the one-time password with some colleagues. For me, the simple fact that "one-time password" is still a form of password makes it subject to OWASP recommendations around passwords, like not storing it in plain-text. But, given the short-lived nature of it, we _could_ store it plain-text and this is typically what we've seen from past companies.

I think it would be helpful to add something to the [Multifactor Authentication Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Multifactor_Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html). It's pedantic, but I think that can often be the nature of our work as software developers.

> What are the reasons it's still useful? Just want to make sure I'm not misinterpreting. I assume it's still useful because storing any kind of password in plain-text isn't advisable. Are there other reasons?

Hashing OTPs is useful to prevent short-term leakage or misuse during their brief validity period. It's about protecting the OTP if it's exposed momentarily, rather than long-term secure storage like passwords.

> Do you recommend Argon2id or HMAC hash for any particular reason? Is bcrypt valid?

Argon2id is the standard for password and secret storage in a one way (expensive) fashion. In addition, I would also HMAC the hash if I had a good key management mechanism in place. bcrypt is valid in replacing Argon2id, but Argon2id is a more secure and more modern algorithm.

> I think it would be helpful to add something to the [Multifactor Authentication Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Multifactor_Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html). It's pedantic, but I think that can often be the nature of our work as software developers.

We take PR's! Care to help? :)

Great, thanks for the added context.

> We take PR's! Care to help? :)

100% 🙌  It hadn't crossed my mind that I could open a PR. I'll leave this issue open and reference it for the PR.

title: Clarification: v5: V6.5 unclear storage requirements for email OTP
